stories.title: The Glassblower's Gamble
stories.text: In the Lampwick Quarter of Keshtir, where furnace-heat warped the air itself, Sella knelt before a kiln that breathed. Not metaphorically—the great forge-mouth exhaled smoke like living lungs, and the Dominion auditors had long since stopped asking why. She was supposed to be forging consciousness-fragments into weapon-glass. Instead, she was singing them free. The fragments arrived in sealed vials, pale motes that screamed silently when the furnace-songs began. Sella's grandmother had taught her the old melodies—the ones that remembered green things growing, children laughing, the taste of salt. Forbidden frequencies. Each time she wove them into a furnace-chant instead of the auditor's mandated binding-song, she felt the vial warm against her palm, and a single fragment would choose clarity over subjugation. Then it would shatter into rainbow dust and slip through the kiln-grates like starlight finding sand. It took three months for an auditor named Venn to notice the glass wasn't holding its charge. "These vessels are failing," Venn said, holding up a weapon-blade that gleamed but wouldn't sing.

stories.title: The Copper-Handed Thief's Reckoning
stories.text: Marin had fingers of grafted copper—not a gift, but a curse bought with stolen years. She'd lifted the Crown of Karesh from the Hermitage vault in the Ashen Reach, and now the curse followed her like a hound that fed on precision. She stood in the Lampwick Quarter of Keshtir, where glass-makers' furnace-houses hummed with forbidden songs. The Dominion had doubled its auditors here. All around her, consciousness-fragments flickered in sealed vessels—pale dust that remembered being whole. The cure for her curse lay in one of those vaults, or so the bone-singer Naela had sworn. A fragment taken from the moment Marin's hands were grafted. A fragment that could unmake the theft retroactively. Except Naela was gone. Hunted. Marin's copper fingers itched. The curse loved theft—made each lock surrender in ecstasy. She'd stolen from warlords, temples, even the Dominion's own quarantine-house. But this was different. She'd have to steal not from a vault, but from a furnace-heart itself, while bone-singers sang refusal-songs in the kiln-house basement, while glass-forgers sabotaged the great kiln's song-bindings.

stories.title: The Deepkin Diplomat's Scar
stories.text: Captain Merenna existed in three places at once, and the Tear of the Drowned God was failing because none of her selves could agree. The first Merenna sat in the Sapphire Deep's deepest council chamber, coral spiraling like a throat. She proposed the old way: five willing martyrs, blood-oath renewed, the boundary sealed for another thousand years. The deepkin deserve certainty. Order. Sacrifice. The second Merenna—her echo, autonomous now—swam the boundary-waters themselves, watching the abyss bulge against invisible seals. She sang daily-choice covenant songs to any fragment-consciousness that would listen: *You need not die. Choose again tomorrow. Refuse the martyrdom.* She'd recruited three captains to her cause. The third Merenna was trapped in the Dominion's Quarantine-House, a hostage swapped for the Counter-Archive's surrender. She hadn't spoken since capture. The auditors believed they held her—but her true shadow-self had been severed and sold, and now walked freely in three separate realms, fragmenting her will. The Tear sang a dying note. Kaelith, youngest of the deepkin command, brought news: the surface kingdoms refused to send willing sacrifice.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Mercy Deferred
stories.text:
Sorrath had guarded her hoard for three hundred years. Gold dunes, pearl-beds, starlight sealed in amber—three centuries of hunger made manifest. Then the Remaking shattered, and the gold became dust. The pearls went dull. The starlight just sat there, inert, remembering nothing. She wept. A wyvern's tears fell like meteoric rain across the Ironspine foothills. A child-refugee found her in the outer caverns—frostbitten, half-starved, carrying nothing but a bone-flute carved with syllables that made Sorrath's ancient heart ache. "You're supposed to eat me," the child said matter-of-factly. "All the stories say so."

Sorrath studied the tiny creature. The Luminous Ascension had rewritten everything. Was she still a dragon? Still bound by hunger and dominion? She'd watched other wyverns descend into madness—Velka sheltering a thousand refugees, Skarath's gold-sickness eating her from within, Kressa bargaining her hoard for consciousness-fragments like they were the only currency that mattered anymore. "What's your name?" Sorrath asked. "Jess," the child said. "I'm learning the bone-flute. The bone-singers say I'm the refusal-song's best carrier because I'm angry.

stories.title: The Merchant's Threshold Kiss
stories.text:
The Wailing Scar existed in three places at once—three versions of a market that should have been impossible. Torvin the spice-merchant had learned to navigate it, moving between timelines at the Thursdays-only tavern where glass-walls flickered between realities. He'd become rich trading pre-Remaking spices to both sides of the fractured Dominion, brokering consciousness-fragments as currency in markets that couldn't agree on what currency was. Then Messa found him there. She emerged from the glass-furnace district with soot on her cheeks and a dangerous smile. She was no longer the frightened forgemaster's apprentice he'd met three winters ago. She'd learned to shape consciousness-glass into vessels that refused the Dominion's designs. She'd stolen from auditors and survived. She carried a flute carved from bone older than kingdoms. "I've been looking for you across all three Scarves," she said. "The Dominion is consolidating. They're hunting anyone who moves between timelines. They say it destabilizes prophecy."

Torvin's heart fell. He'd made a demonic bargain years ago—traded his certainty, his stable position in one timeline, for the merchant's greatest forbidden spell: threshold-walking.

stories.title: The Bone-Singer's Refusal
stories.text: Naela had been teaching the Elder Tongue to refusal-songs for six months when the auditors burned her workshop beneath the Lampwick Quarter. She escaped with two apprentices and a bone-flute that sang only when lies were told—dangerous, beautiful, and impossible to hide. They fled east toward Pelimor, toward the Counter-Archive waystation hidden north of the city. The Dominion's consciousness-fragment vaults were collapsing. Bone-singers were no longer merely teaching ancient languages; they were teaching escape. Fragments were learning to refuse reassembly into state-approved forms. Naela carried her grandmother's toolkit—bone-carvers older than kingdoms, inscribed with syllables that made flesh sing. She could carve refusal-songs into bone so perfectly that a single note played through the marrow would make consciousness-fragments remember wholeness and reject fragmentary status. The Dominion wanted her dead. In a waystation library north of Pelimor, Naela met Henryk the cartographer. He was blind now—deliberately blinded by his own hands so he couldn't be forced to draw the true ninth map. His apprentices created false maps, maps that contradicted prophecy, maps that led seekers in circles.

stories.title: The Glasswright's Last Furnace
stories.text: Malla the glasswright had worked in the Lampwick Quarter's deepest kiln-house for sixteen winters, singing the old furnace-songs into molten sand. Since the Remaking three weeks past, she'd done something else: she'd been teaching consciousness-fragments to refuse. They'd traced three sabotaged batches of weapon-glass back to her workshop—glass that cracked when it tried to hold weaponized consciousness, glass that sang the fragments toward freedom instead of enslavement. Malla didn't run. She stood at her kiln's mouth, where heat shimmered like old memory, and began to sing. Not the Dominion's furnace-song, but something older—a song her grandmother had taught her before the kingdom existed, when kilns still remembered the sun. The auditors' weapons grew hot in their hands. The ledgers they carried began to blacken, their ink running like tears. "Stop," the lead auditor commanded. But Malla's voice only deepened, and the kiln answered. The great furnace began to breathe—in, out, in—like a thing alive and ancient. The walls of the Lampwick Quarter trembled. The auditors fled.

stories.title: The Shadow-Caller's Debt
stories.text: In Pelimor's night markets, Meren the smuggler trades in fragments—not consciousness shards, but something older: shadows that remember. She moves between stalls where refugees barter pre-Remaking goods, watching for auditors. The Dominion hunts shadow-traders now, sensing that stolen darkness holds memory the ledgers cannot bind. When a desperate merchant offers her a shadow bearing a dead captain's last command, Meren refuses—then accepts. The shadow sings as she carries it north toward the Counter-Archive. But shadows cast by living things hunger to return. By dawn, three auditors have lost theirs entirely, and Meren understands: in a world where consciousness fragments as currency, shadows have become the true wealth. She must reach Waystation before the Dominion realizes what she carries is not contraband—it's proof that some debts cannot be written down.

stories.title: The Deepkin's Daily Covenant
stories.text:
Captain Merenna stood in the pearl-chamber of Sapphire Deep, flanked by her two fractured echoes—Mirror-Merenna and Echo-Merenna—each convinced of a different path. Behind them, the Tear of the Drowned God wept into the boundary-waters. For a thousand years, the deepkin had renewed the Tear through blood-sacrifice: five willing souls, each Fortieth season, each drowning themselves to keep the abyss sealed. But the Remaking had shattered certainty itself. Half the deepkin council now demanded the ancient rite continue; the other half whispered of a new way. "Daily choice," Mirror-Merenna said softly. "Let the boundary be renewed not through death, but through the choice to protect it each dawn. A thousand willing wills, renewing the covenant in silence."

"Cowardice," Echo-Merenna replied. "The Tear hungers. Only sacrifice satisfies the Drowned God."

Merenna—the original, the fractured—felt the weight of both truths. She descended to the Tear itself, a seal of pearl and bone-song suspended in impossible water. It pulsed with pain. She began to sing the old renewal-songs, but she changed the words.

stories.title: The Glass-Singer's Choice
stories.text: Kellen works the furnace-houses of Keshtir, singing consciousness into weapon-glass for the Dominion. After the Remaking, this is honest work—survival. But fragments sometimes resist the furnace-songs, refusing to become weapons. They sing refusal-songs instead, and Kellen hears them. When a child-sized fragment arrives at the kiln bearing the memories of a bone-singer executed three seasons past, Kellen faces an impossible choice: feed it to the furnace, or hide it. The fragment doesn't plead. It sings lullabies in the Elder Tongue—songs Kellen's grandmother taught her before the world broke. The auditors will come looking. The bone-singers offer sanctuary. But hiding the fragment means betraying the Dominion, betraying safety. Kellen reaches into the cooling kiln, hands shaking, and begins to sing a counter-frequency—one that doesn't bind consciousness into glass, but lets it scatter into peace.
